modules.title: Mastery check and report
goals: Show what you can do on every objective, on questions you have not seen.
Read your report and see what to review before the lecture.

segments.title: About the mastery check
segments.body:
Could you model a network as a graph, say when BFS fits, trace it, write it and test it, on your own? The graphs lecture assumes you can. This check shows you now, while there is still time to fix a gap, rather than in the lecture.

**What to expect.** There are 28 questions on the eight objectives, all of them new to you. Allow about 55 minutes. You can stop at any time and carry on later from where you left off: your answers are kept.

**One answer each.** Each question counts once: your first answer is the one your report uses, so check it before you send it. Hints 1 and 2 are there if you need them. Hints 3 and 4 give the answer away, so this check doesn't offer them.

**Your report** shows each objective separately: **met independently** or **not yet**. You're ready for the lecture when nothing is “not yet”. If an objective is, you get a short review path for it: it teaches the idea again, gives you practice with every hint, and ends with fresh questions. Meeting the objective there after hint 3 or 4 counts as **met with support**.

config.prompt: Which of these is a data structure?

options.label: Visiting every page of a website by following links
A bus timetable listing every stop and the time the bus gets there
How a sat-nav works out which turn you should take next

feedback.c: Not quite. That's a graph traversal: it visits pages by following links, so it is something done, not something kept. Ask: does it hold information, or is it a method for doing something?
feedback.e: Not quite. That's an algorithm: a method the sat-nav follows to decide. It doesn't hold the information itself. Ask: does it hold information, or is it a method for doing something?

hints.body: Ask of each: does it hold information, or is it a way of doing something?
Something that keeps information organised is a data structure. A method, or a way of moving through something, is not.
Choosing a turn and visiting pages are both things done.
Answer: the bus timetable, which holds the stops and times.

config.prompt: Which of these is an algorithm?

options.label: A map of the stations on a train line and the tracks between them
A playlist, in the order the songs will play
The rules for deciding whether a year is a leap year

feedback.c: Not quite. That's a graph. A map of stations and tracks is a graph, which is a data structure. Find the option that is a method for working something out.
feedback.e: Not quite. The songs are in an order, but the playlist only holds them, and something that holds information is a data structure. Ask: does it hold information, or is it a method for doing something?

hints.body: An algorithm is a method that solves a problem.
Something that only holds information is a data structure, however it is ordered. An algorithm is a method you can follow.
Which option tells you how to work something out?
Answer: the rules for deciding whether a year is a leap year.

config.prompt: Match each term to its example. One example matches none of them.

left.label: Data structure
Algorithm
Graph traversal

right.label: A bar chart of the test marks in a class
Checking every room in a building by walking through its doors
The method for working out a 15% tip on a bill
A phone's list of recent calls, newest first

feedback.t3: Not quite. A data structure keeps information organised so a program can use it, like a phone's list of recent calls. Find the example that holds information for a program.
feedback.t4: Not quite. An algorithm is a method that solves a problem, like working out a tip. Find the example that is a way of working something out.
feedback.t2: Not quite. A traversal goes to every one of a set of connected things by moving along the connections, like walking through every room by its doors. Find the example about visiting everything.

hints.body: One example holds information, one is a way of working something out, one visits connected things, and one is none of these.
A bar chart is the everyday kind of graph, a picture of values: it is none of these terms.
Walking through every room by its doors is visiting connected things.
Answer: data structure → the list of recent calls; algorithm → working out a tip; graph traversal → checking every room.

config.prompt: A municipal inspector starts at the waterworks and follows the pipes until every reservoir they can reach has been checked. Which term describes what the inspector does?

options.label: A data structure
A graph
Building a graph
A graph traversal

feedback.e: Not quite. The pipes and reservoirs are a graph, but the inspector isn't the pipes: they move along them. Ask: is this something that stores, or something that is done?
feedback.f: Not quite. The pipes and reservoirs could be stored in a data structure, but the inspector isn't storing anything: they move along the pipes. Ask: is this something that stores, or something that is done?
feedback.g: Not quite. Nothing new is added: the pipes and reservoirs are already there, and the inspector moves along them. Ask: is the inspector adding connections, or following them?

hints.body: Ask: is the inspector something that stores, or something that is done?
The pipes and reservoirs are the graph. What is the inspector doing to it?
The inspector goes to every reservoir they can reach by moving along the pipes.
Answer: a graph traversal.

config.prompt: Which statement is true?

options.label: BFS is a data structure that stores all of a graph's vertices and edges.
BFS is an algorithm that traverses a graph, which is a data structure.
A graph is an algorithm, and BFS is the data it uses.

feedback.b: Not quite. BFS doesn't store anything; it's a list of steps. Decide which is the algorithm and which is the data structure.
feedback.c: Not quite. That's the wrong way round. The graph holds the data; BFS is the algorithm that visits it. Swap the roles.

hints.body: One of BFS and graph stores data; the other is a list of steps.
A graph stores vertices and edges.
BFS is a list of steps that visits a graph.
Answer: BFS is an algorithm that traverses a graph, which is a data structure.

config.prompt: Taps in a garden, joined by hoses. The taps are the kitchen tap (P), the fountain tap (Q), the lawn tap (R) and the shed tap (S). Hoses join P–Q, Q–R and R–S, and water can flow either way along a hose. Each marker below describes one part of this graph. Match each marker to its name in the graph: is it a vertex or an edge, and which one?

left.label: Marker 1: the tap between the kitchen tap and the lawn tap
Marker 2: the hose from the kitchen tap to the fountain tap
Marker 3: what carries water to the shed tap

feedback.1: Check marker 1. It describes one of the things in the graph, so it is a vertex. Use the names and the hose list to work out which one, then give its letter.
feedback.2: Check marker 2. It describes a hose between two things, so it is an edge, named by the letters of its two ends. Use the names and the list to find both ends.
feedback.3: Check marker 3. It describes a hose between two things, so it is an edge, named by the letters of its two ends. Use the names and the list to find both ends.

hints.body: Taps are vertices. Hoses are edges.
Name an edge by the two vertices at its ends.
Look up each name's letter in the prompt: the kitchen tap is P and the lawn tap is R. Then use the hose list.
Answer: 1 = Vertex Q, 2 = Edge P–Q, 3 = Edge R–S.

config.prompt: Rooms on a floor, joined by doorways. The rooms are the kitchen (P), the lounge (Q), the music room (S) and the nursery (T). Doorways join P–Q, P–S, Q–T and S–T, and you can walk through a doorway either way. Each marker below describes one part of this graph. Match each marker to its name in the graph: is it a vertex or an edge, and which one?

left.label: Marker 1: the doorway between the kitchen and the music room
Marker 2: the nursery
Marker 3: what joins the lounge and the nursery

feedback.1: Check marker 1. It describes a doorway between two things, so it is an edge, named by the letters of its two ends. Use the names and the list to find both ends.
feedback.2: Check marker 2. It describes one of the things in the graph, so it is a vertex. Use the names and the doorway list to work out which one, then give its letter.
feedback.3: Check marker 3. It describes a doorway between two things, so it is an edge, named by the letters of its two ends. Use the names and the list to find both ends.

hints.body: Rooms are vertices. Doorways are edges.
Name an edge by the two vertices at its ends.
Look up each name's letter in the prompt: the kitchen is P and the music room is S.
Answer: 1 = Edge P–S, 2 = Vertex T, 3 = Edge Q–T.

config.prompt: A one-way route through three stops: the market (X), the bridge (Y) and the depot (Z). One-way roads go X → Y and Y → Z: you can only drive them in that direction. Each marker below describes one part of this graph. Match each marker to its name in the graph: is it a vertex or an edge, and which one?

left.label: Marker 1: the road from the market to the bridge
Marker 2: what you reach after driving on from the bridge
Marker 3: what you drive along to leave the bridge

feedback.1: Check marker 1. It describes a one-way road between two places, so it is an edge, named from where it starts to where it ends. Use the names and the list to find both ends and the way it goes.
feedback.2: Check marker 2. It describes one of the things in the graph, so it is a vertex. Use the names and the one-way road list to work out which one, then give its letter.
feedback.3: Check marker 3. It describes a one-way road between two places, so it is an edge, named from where it starts to where it ends. Use the names and the list to find both ends and the way it goes.

hints.body: Stops are vertices. One-way roads are edges.
Name an edge by the two vertices at its ends.
Look up each name's letter in the prompt: the market is X and the bridge is Y. A one-way edge is named from where it starts to where it ends.
Answer: 1 = Edge X → Y, 2 = Vertex Z, 3 = Edge Y → Z.

config.prompt: Is each graph directed or undirected? Decide from what each connection means.

left.label: A flat's money: who owes money to whom. Amo owes Bongi, and Chris owes Bongi.
Houses on a street, and which houses share a wall. House 1 shares a wall with House 2, and House 2 with House 3.
TikTok follows between Dudu, Ewan and Fezi. Every one of them follows the other two, and each follow is its own link.
Learners in an exam, and who sat next to whom.

feedback.owes: Not quite. Owing money goes one way: Amo owes Bongi, but Bongi doesn't owe Amo. Ask: if this connection exists, must the reverse one exist too?
feedback.walls: Not quite. A shared wall belongs to both houses: if House 1 shares a wall with House 2, House 2 shares it with House 1. Ask: could this connection exist one way only?
feedback.mutual: Not quite. Each follow is a one-way link, even when it's returned, so Dudu → Ewan and Ewan → Dudu are two separate arrows. A graph of one-way links is directed. Ask: is each single connection one-way?
feedback.seats: Not quite. If Thabo sat next to Lindiwe, Lindiwe sat next to Thabo. Ask: could this connection exist one way only?

hints.body: Ask of each connection: if it joins X to Y, must it also join Y to X?
If the reverse must always exist, the graph is undirected. If one can exist without the other, it is directed.
Watch the follows: every pair follows each other, but each follow is still one arrow.
Answer: owing money = directed; shared walls = undirected; TikTok follows = directed; sitting next to = undirected.

config.prompt: In a class WhatsApp group, the app keeps a record of who has replied to whose message. Which graph models who has replied to whom?

options.label: Vertices: learners. Edges: replies. Undirected, because a reply is part of a chat between two people.
Vertices: learners. Edges: replies. Directed, because a reply can go one way without one coming back.
Vertices: messages. Edges: the learners who wrote them. Directed, because a message has one writer.
Vertices: learners. Edges: the messages each learner sent to the group. Directed, as each is sent.

feedback.f: Not quite. Two people are involved, but that doesn't make a connection two-way: a learner can reply to another's message without a reply coming back. Ask: if this edge exists, must the reverse one exist too?
feedback.g: Not quite. A message isn't joined to another message here: the replies join learners. The learners are the things in this graph. Ask: what does each reply connect?
feedback.h: Not quite. A message sent to the whole group doesn't join two particular learners, so it can't be an edge. An edge always has two ends. Ask: which connection always joins exactly two learners?

hints.body: Ask: what are the things, and what joins two of them?
The vertices are the things being connected, and each edge joins exactly two of them.
The learners are the vertices and the replies are the edges. Now: if one learner replied to another, must the other have replied too?
Answer: Vertices: learners. Edges: replies. Directed, because a reply can go one way without one coming back.

config.prompt: In a molecule of water, the oxygen atom is bonded to each of the two hydrogen atoms. A chemist wants a graph of which atoms are bonded to which. Which graph models it?

options.label: Vertices: atoms. Edges: bonds. Directed, because each bond goes from one atom to the other atom.
Vertices: bonds. Edges: the atoms at their two ends. Undirected, because each bond has two atoms.
Vertices: molecules. Edges: the atoms in them. Undirected, because each atom is in one molecule.
Vertices: atoms. Edges: bonds. Undirected, because being bonded works the same from either side.

feedback.e: Not quite. A bond joins two atoms equally: if oxygen is bonded to hydrogen, hydrogen is bonded to oxygen. Something touching both ends doesn't give it an arrow. Ask: could this connection exist one way only?
feedback.g: Not quite. That swaps them. A bond joins two atoms, so the bond is the edge and the atoms are the vertices. Ask: which one joins the other two?
feedback.h: Not quite. There is only one molecule here, and the question is about which atoms are bonded. Ask: what are the things being joined?

hints.body: Ask: what are the things, and what joins two of them?
The vertices are the things being connected, and each edge joins exactly two of them.
Atoms are the vertices and bonds are the edges. Is being bonded ever one-way?
Answer: Vertices: atoms. Edges: bonds. Undirected, because being bonded works the same from either side.

activities.title: Objective 3 · item 3 of 4: build the model

config.prompt: Building a house: the foundations must be finished before the walls go up, and the walls before the roof. A builder wants a graph of which job must be finished before which. Build the graph: match each part of the situation to what it becomes in the graph. Some choices fit nothing.

left.label: The foundations, the walls and the roof
“The foundations must be finished before the walls”
The way that link points
The whole graph

right.label: A directed graph: each edge goes one way
From the walls to the foundations
From the foundations to the walls
An undirected graph: each edge goes both ways

feedback.p1: Not quite. The jobs are the things being linked, so each job is a vertex. Ask: which are the things, and which are the links between them?
feedback.p2: Not quite. “Must be finished before” links two jobs, so it is an edge between their vertices. Ask: is it a thing, or a link between two things?
feedback.p3: Not quite. The foundations come first and the walls wait for them, so the arrow goes from the foundations to the walls. Ask: which job must be done first?
feedback.p4: Not quite. “Foundations before walls” doesn't work the other way round, so each edge goes one way and the graph is directed. Ask: does the link work both ways?

hints.body: First find the things being linked, then the links between them.
A link that works only one way needs an arrow. Does “must be finished before” work both ways?
The jobs are the vertices and each “must be finished before” link is an edge. The arrow starts at the job that must be done first.
Answer: the jobs → vertices; “foundations before walls” → an edge; the way it points → from the foundations to the walls; the whole graph → a directed graph.

config.prompt: The exams office says two subjects clash when at least one learner takes both, so they can't be written at the same time. It wants a graph of which subjects clash. Which graph models it?

options.label: Vertices: learners. Edges: the subjects they take. Undirected, as a learner takes many subjects.
Vertices: subjects. Edges: clashes. Directed, because one subject is written before the other.
Vertices: subjects. Edges: clashes. Undirected, because a clash is shared by both of its subjects.
Vertices: exam sessions. Edges: subjects. Undirected, because each session holds a few of the subjects.

feedback.h: Not quite. The learners cause the clashes, but the office wants to know which subjects clash. A clash joins two subjects. Ask: which things does each clash join?
feedback.e: Not quite. If Maths clashes with Physics, Physics clashes with Maths: nothing has been written yet, so there is no first or later. Ask: can a clash go one way only?
feedback.g: Not quite. The sessions are what the office will choose later; the graph shows which subjects clash. Ask: which things does each clash join?

hints.body: Ask: what are the things, and what joins two of them?
The vertices are the things being connected, and each edge joins exactly two of them.
Subjects are the vertices and clashes are the edges. If Maths clashes with Physics, does Physics clash with Maths?
Answer: Vertices: subjects. Edges: clashes. Undirected, because a clash is shared by both of its subjects.

config.prompt: A word game: turn COLD into WARM by changing one letter at a time, and every step must be a real word (COLD, CORD, CARD, WARD, WARM). You want the fewest changes. Is BFS a good fit? Choose the answer with the right reason.

options.label: Yes. Our BFS orders the neighbours of a vertex alphabetically, and that keeps the ladder short.
No. BFS will follow one path of word changes to its end, so its first chain may be long.
Yes. Taking words as vertices, BFS finishes each distance before starting the next: shortest ladder.

feedback.g: Not quite. Alphabetical order only decides which neighbour joins the queue first. The chain is short because BFS reaches words ring by ring: every word one change away, then two. Ask: what makes BFS find the fewest edges?
feedback.h: Not quite. That describes depth-first search. BFS finishes every word one change away before any word two changes away, so the first time it reaches WARM it has used the fewest changes. Ask: does BFS go wide or deep?

hints.body: First ask: are there things joined by connections?
Think of a graph where one letter-change joins two words. What does the puzzle want as small as possible?
It wants the fewest changes, and each change is one edge. BFS reaches vertices in rings, one edge further out each time. Does that give the fewest edges?
Answer: Yes. Taking words as vertices, BFS finishes each distance before starting the next: shortest ladder.

config.prompt: Find the cheapest flight route, where every flight has a different price. Is BFS a good fit? Choose the answer with the right reason.

options.label: Yes. BFS finds the path with the fewest flights, and that path is always the cheapest one.
No. BFS counts the edges on a route, not the prices, so the fewest may cost more.
Yes. The queue lets the cheapest flight out first, so BFS reaches the best price.

feedback.b: Not quite. BFS does find the fewest flights, but two cheap flights can cost less than one expensive one. Ask: does this problem count edges, or add up prices?
feedback.e: Not quite. A queue is first in, first out: it keeps vertices in the order they were found, not in order of price. Ask: does this problem count edges, or add up prices?

hints.body: First ask: are there things joined by connections?
There is a graph: airports joined by flights. But what is the problem trying to make smallest: the number of flights, or something else?
It wants the lowest total price, and each flight has its own price. BFS counts flights, not prices. Could two cheap flights cost less than one dear one?
Answer: No. BFS counts the edges on a route, not the prices, so the fewest may cost more.

config.prompt: Check whether every computer in a lab network can be reached from the server. Is BFS a good fit? Choose the answer with the right reason.

options.label: No. BFS will only follow one path to one computer, and then it stops looking.
Yes. BFS reaches only the computers with a path from the server; the rest are cut off.
No. BFS reaches every vertex from the start, so no computer would ever look cut off.

feedback.a: Not quite. BFS doesn't stop at one path: it keeps going until the queue is empty, so it visits every vertex it can reach from the start. Ask: what has BFS visited when it finishes?
feedback.e: Not quite. BFS only follows edges from the start, so a computer with no path from the server is never found, and that missing computer is what you're looking for. Ask: can BFS reach a vertex that no path leads to?

hints.body: First ask: are there things joined by connections?
Is this about the fewest edges, or about whether something can be reached at all?
It asks which computers can be reached from the server. BFS from the server finds exactly those. What happens to a computer with no path from the server?
Answer: Yes. BFS reaches only the computers with a path from the server; the rest are cut off.

config.prompt: Work out the average mark of a class. Is BFS a good fit? Choose the answer with the right reason.

options.label: No. There are no edges between marks to follow: a plain loop gives the average.
Yes. BFS will reach every student, adding up all the marks along each path it takes.
No. Taking the neighbours of each vertex alphabetically, as BFS does, changes the average.

feedback.a: Not quite. BFS visits vertices by following edges, and marks have no edges between them. A loop that adds each mark does the job. Ask: are there connections to follow?
feedback.h: Not quite. The order you add numbers in never changes their average. BFS doesn't fit because there are no connections to follow. Ask: are there connections to follow?

hints.body: First ask: are there things joined by connections?
Is there a graph here? What would join one mark to another?
The marks are just numbers in a list: nothing joins one mark to another. Does the problem need edges to follow?
Answer: No. There are no edges between marks to follow: a plain loop gives the average.

activities.title: Objective 5 · item 1 of 1: trace BFS from A, one row each time a vertex leaves the queue

hints.body: Each row starts by taking the vertex at the front of the previous queue.
Add the current vertex's neighbours that haven't been found yet to the back of the queue, in alphabetical order. A vertex is found when it joins the queue and visited when it leaves.
The first row: A leaves; the queue becomes D, F.
Answer: order A, D, F, C, E, B, G. Queues after each row: [D, F]; [F, C, E]; [C, E, B]; [E, B, G]; [B, G]; [G]; [].

activities.title: Objective 6 · item 1 of 2: put BFS in order, taking neighbours in alphabetical order as this course does

hints.body: Before the loop you need three things: the set of vertices found so far, the queue of vertices waiting, and the order list.
While a vertex is waiting, take the one at the front of the queue and add it to the order.

For each neighbour w in sorted(graph.adjacency[u]) that isn't in the found set yet: add it to the found set, then to the back of waiting. Return the order. Four lines don't belong: pop(), set(), the loop that doesn't sort (a BFS could take neighbours in any order, but this course takes them alphabetically) and return found.

Answer: from collections import deque; def bfs(graph, start):; found = {start}; waiting = deque([start]); order = []; while waiting:; u = waiting.popleft(); order.append(u); for w in sorted(graph.adjacency[u]):; if w not in found:; found.add(w); waiting.append(w); return order.

activities.title: Objective 6 · item 2 of 2: fill in the missing parts of BFS

config.code:
from collections import deque


def bfs(graph, start):
    # Return the vertices in the order BFS visits them from start,
    # taking neighbours in alphabetical order.
    # This version skips a neighbour it has already found with continue.
    found = __1__
    queue = deque([start])
    order = []
    while len(queue) > 0:
        v = queue.__2__
        order.append(v)
        for n in __3__:
            if n in found:
                continue
            found.add(n)
            queue.append(n)
    return __4__

1.set(): Not quite. The start vertex is in the queue but not in the found set, which holds every vertex found so far, so a neighbour can add it to the queue again and it is visited twice. Start with the start vertex already in the found set.
1.{}: Not quite. {} is an empty dictionary, not an empty set, so found.add(n) stops with an error. A set holding the start vertex is written {start}.

2.pop(): Not quite. pop() takes the newest vertex, from the back of the queue, so BFS goes deep instead of wide. Take the vertex that has waited longest, from the front, with popleft().
2.pop(0): Not quite. A deque's pop takes no position, so pop(0) stops with an error. A deque takes the vertex at the front with popleft().

3.graph.adjacency[v]: Not quite. That takes v's neighbours in the order their edges were added, not alphabetically. Loop over sorted(graph.adjacency[v]).
3.sorted(graph.adjacency[start]): Not quite. That looks at the start's neighbours every time, not the neighbours of v, the vertex that just left the queue, so BFS never gets past the first ring. Loop over v's neighbours, sorted.

4.found: Not quite. found is a set, and a set has no order. bfs must return the list of vertices in the order BFS visited them.
4.queue: Not quite. The loop only ends when the queue is empty, so the queue has nothing left in it. Return the list of vertices in the order BFS visited them.

hints.body: You need a found set, a queue and an order list before the loop.
BFS takes the vertex that has waited longest, from the front of the queue.
The start vertex is in the found set from the beginning, neighbours are taken in alphabetical order, and the order is a list.
Answer: blank 1 is {start}, blank 2 is popleft(), blank 3 is sorted(graph.adjacency[v]), and blank 4 is order.

activities.title: Objective 7 · item 1 of 4: fix the faulty BFS

config.prompt: Our BFS takes each vertex's neighbours in alphabetical order, as in module 4: a convention this course uses so that everyone's traces agree, not a rule of BFS. On a graph whose edges were added in the order A–C, A–B, B–D, C–E, our BFS from A gives A, B, C, D, E, but this one gives A, C, B, E, D. Replace the faulty line with a correction.

feedback.9: Not quite. This loop takes v's neighbours in the order their edges were added, so C, added first, joins the queue before B. That is still breadth-first, but our BFS takes neighbours in alphabetical order, the course's convention so that traces agree. Sort v's own list of neighbours.

hints.body: Compare the two orders. Which vertices come out in a different order, and are they in the same ring?
Look at the line that loops over v's neighbours. In what order does it take them?
It takes them in the order their edges were added, so C comes before B. Our BFS takes each vertex's neighbours in alphabetical order: the course's convention, not a rule of BFS.
Answer: replace for n in graph.adjacency[v]: with for n in sorted(graph.adjacency[v]):, which sorts v's own neighbours.

activities.title: Objective 7 · item 2 of 4: fix the faulty BFS

config.prompt: This BFS gives the wrong order even on simple graphs. Replace the faulty line with a correction.

feedback.7: Not quite. pop() takes the newest vertex, from the back, so this explores depth first. BFS must take the vertex that has waited longest, from the front.

hints.body: The order is wrong even on simple graphs. Which line takes a vertex from the queue?
BFS must take the vertex that has waited longest.
pop() takes the newest vertex, from the back.
Answer: change v = queue.pop() to v = queue.popleft().

activities.title: Objective 7 · item 3 of 4: choose the tests that catch the bug

config.prompt: This BFS has a bug. Choose every test case it fails: each one is a graph, a start vertex and the order a correct BFS visits it in.

feedback.cycle: R can be reached along two routes, from P and from Q. When Q looks at R, R is still waiting in the queue and isn't in the found set yet, so it joins again: the faulty version gives P, Q, R, R and fails this test.
feedback.tree: A tree has only one route to each vertex, so no vertex can be found a second time while it waits: the faulty version passes this test.
feedback.added-backwards: The faulty version still sorts each vertex's neighbours, and A's neighbours each have only one route to them, so nothing is added twice: it passes this test.
feedback.fork-join: There's no cycle here, but D can be reached along two routes, through B and through C. When C looks at D, D is still waiting and isn't in the found set yet, so it joins the queue again. The faulty version fails this test.
feedback.back-to-start: This graph has a cycle, but it only leads back to A, which has already left the queue and is in the found set. No vertex is reached twice while it waits, so the faulty version passes this test.
feedback.two-islands: BFS from B never reaches A, and B, C and D lie on a path with one route to each vertex. Nothing is found twice, so the faulty version passes this test.

hints.body: This version adds a vertex to the found set only when it leaves the queue, not when it joins.
A vertex still waiting in the queue isn't in the found set yet, so a second vertex can add it again.

That needs two routes to the same vertex, with the second found while the vertex still waits. A cycle isn't needed, and a cycle that only leads back to the start isn't enough: the start has already left the queue.
Answer: Tests 1 and 4. The faulty version passes the other four.

activities.title: Objective 7 · item 4 of 4: choose the tests that catch the bug

activities.title: Quick recall: a graph that tests BFS

config.prompt: A BFS marks a vertex as found only when it leaves the queue. Which kind of test graph would show that it can visit a vertex twice?

options.label: A graph with one vertex and no edges
A graph where one vertex can be reached along two routes
A straight path with no branches
A graph in two pieces, with no edge between them

solution.explanation: Correct. If a vertex can be reached along two routes, a second vertex can find it while it still waits in the queue, and this BFS adds it again. What matters is the two routes, not whether the graph has a cycle.

feedback.single: Not quite. With one vertex there is nothing to find twice. Look for a graph where two vertices can both find the same vertex.
feedback.line: Not quite. On a path there is only one route to each vertex, so this bug can't add one twice. Look for a graph where two vertices can both find the same vertex.
feedback.islands: Not quite. Two separate pieces expose a different bug, one that adds vertices BFS can't reach. Each piece here could still have one route to each vertex. Look for a graph where two vertices can both find the same vertex.

hints.body: Where could BFS meet the same vertex a second time?
This BFS only counts a vertex as found once it leaves the queue, so a vertex still waiting can be found again.
That needs two vertices that can both find the same vertex, while it still waits in the queue.
Answer: a graph where one vertex can be reached along two routes.

config.prompt: A bus network joins stops with these routes, each one bus ride: P–Q, P–R, Q–S, R–S, R–T, S–U, T–U and U–V. How many rides does the trip from P to V take, at the fewest?

options.label: 3 rides
4 rides
5 rides
6 rides

feedback.b: Not quite. V is joined only to U, and U is 3 rides from P, so V is one more. Ask: in which ring of BFS does V appear?
feedback.a: Not quite. 5 counts the stops on a trip such as P, Q, S, U, V, not the rides between them. Each ride is one edge. Count the edges.
feedback.d: Not quite. 6 is how many stops BFS visits before V (P, Q, R, S, T, U), not how far V is. Ask: in which ring does V appear?

hints.body: Run BFS from P and note how many rides away each stop is.
Q and R are 1 ride away. Which stops are 2 rides away?
S and T are 2 away, U is 3 away. Where does V come in?
Answer: 4 rides, for example P, Q, S, U, V.

config.prompt: Two-way roads join six towns: J–K, J–L, K–M, L–M, L–N, M–P and N–P. BFS runs from J, takes neighbours in alphabetical order, and records which vertex found each one. Following those records back from P, which route does it give?

options.label: J, L, N, P
J, K, M, P
J, L, M, P

feedback.c: Not quite. J, L, N, P also has 3 edges, but it isn't the route BFS records: M leaves the queue before N, so M finds P first. Ask: which vertex took P into the queue?
feedback.b: Not quite. L doesn't find M: K leaves the queue before L and finds M first. Ask: who found M?

hints.body: Write down the order BFS visits the vertices.
For each vertex, note which vertex put it in the queue.
K found M. Which of M and N leaves the queue first?
Answer: J, K, M, P.

config.prompt: In a graph where every edge counts the same, why does the route BFS records always have the fewest edges?

options.label: It takes every vertex one edge away out of the queue before any two away, so it first reaches each by fewest edges.
Our BFS takes the neighbours of each vertex in alphabetical order, which leads it straight towards the goal.
BFS compares every possible route from the start vertex to the goal and then keeps whichever one turned out shortest.
BFS marks each vertex as found, so it never goes round a cycle, and that keeps every route it records short.

feedback.b: Not quite. BFS never compares routes: each vertex joins the queue once. The guarantee comes from the order it works in. Ask: what does BFS finish before it moves further out?
feedback.c: Not quite. Marking vertices stops BFS repeating work, but depth-first search marks them too and can still find a long route first. Ask: in what order do vertices leave the queue?
feedback.a: Not quite. Alphabetical order only breaks ties between neighbours, and BFS doesn't know where the goal is. Ask: in what order do vertices leave the queue?

hints.body: Think about the order in which vertices leave the queue.
Which vertices does BFS finish before it looks any further from the start?
So when BFS first reaches a vertex, could a shorter route still be waiting?
Answer: it takes every vertex one edge away out of the queue before any two away, so it first reaches each by fewest edges.

config.prompt: BFS from S reaches T for the first time while it is working through the vertices 3 edges from S. A friend says there is a route from S to T with only 2 edges. Who is right?

options.label: BFS. A 2-edge route would mean BFS found T sooner.
Your friend, because BFS stops at the first route it meets and never goes back to check for a shorter one later.
Either could be: BFS finds a short route, but it only promises the shortest one when the graph has no cycles at all.

feedback.c: Not quite. BFS doesn't need to go back: it finishes every vertex 1 edge away before any 2 away, so a 2-edge route would have put T in the queue earlier. Ask: when would BFS have found T?
feedback.a: Not quite. Cycles don't change the guarantee: BFS marks each vertex it finds and still works ring by ring. Ask: if T were 2 edges away, which vertex would have found it, and when?

hints.body: If T were 2 edges from S, which kind of vertex would be joined to T?
When does BFS take the vertices 1 edge from S out of the queue?
Each of them would have put T in the queue during the 1-edge ring.
Answer: BFS. A 2-edge route would mean BFS found T sooner.
